pos: n. (the state or practice of living by begging; as a religious principle, the mendicant orders' rule of corporate poverty)
etymology: Latin mendicare, to beg, from mendicus, a beggar; itself perhaps from mendum, a defect or want.
biblical_def: Mendicancy is living by what others give because one owns nothing to live on. As a condition it is pitiable and Scripture treats it so, with compassion for the beggar at the gate — “whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask alms of them that entered into the temple” (Act 3:2) — and for blind Bartimaeus who “sat by the highway side begging” (Mar 10:46). As a chosen religious principle, which is what the thirteenth-century friars made it, mendicancy is harder to defend. Its warrant was drawn from Christ's charge to the Twelve: “Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses” (Mat 10:9). But that was a commission for a particular mission, and Paul, sent on a wider one, worked with his hands precisely so as not to beg: “Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you” (2Th 3:8). The Psalmist moreover treats begging as the mark of the forsaken, not of the holy. The friars' instinct — that a preacher should not be rich, and should not be owned by those who feed him — was sound. The vow that made destitution itself a merit was not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mendicancy as beggary, a state of begging; mendicant as begging, poor to a state of beggary, and as a noun a beggar or one of the begging fraternities of the Romish church; and beg as to ask alms or charity.
webster_full: MENDICANCY, n. Beggary; a state of begging; the life of a beggar.
MENDICANT, a. Begging; poor to a state of beggary; practising beggary.
MENDICANT, n. A beggar; one that lives by begging; also, one of the begging fraternities in the Romish church.
BEG, v.i. To ask alms or charity; to practice begging; to live by asking alms.
ALMS, n. Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food, or clothing.
scriptures: Act 3:2
And a certain man lame from his mother's womb was carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask alms of them that entered into the temple;
And they came to Jericho: and as he went out of Jericho with his disciples and a great number of people, blind Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, sat by the highway side begging.
Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you:
I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.
corruption_summary: Living by begging, made a religious vow: compassion owed to the beggar, but destitution turned into merit is a doctrine Scripture does not teach.
corruption_paragraphs: The medieval corruption was to read a temporary commission as a permanent counsel of perfection, and then to attach merit to it. Christ's “for the workman is worthy of his meat” (Mat 10:10) establishes that a minister may be supported; it does not establish that he must own nothing. Paul draws the balance himself — he had the right to be supported and often declined it — and his rule for the ordinary Christian is the opposite of mendicancy: “let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth” (Eph 4:28).

The modern misuse runs the other way, treating any voluntary simplicity as neurosis and any dependence as failure. That is no better. The principle to recover is contentment, which is neither destitution nor accumulation: “having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8), and “give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me” (Pro 30:8).
roots_summary: Latin mendicus, a beggar; Hebrew ebyon (H34), needy; Hebrew sha'al (H7592), to ask; Greek ptochos (G4434), a crouching beggar; Greek epaiteo (G1871), to beg.
roots_lines: Latin mendicus — a beggar; the root of both “mendicant” and “mendicancy”.
Hebrew ebyon (H34) — needy, destitute, one who must ask; the Psalter's poor man.
Greek ptochos (G4434) — a beggar, one crouching for alms; “Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith” (Jam 2:5).
Greek epaiteo (G1871) — to beg; “to beg I am ashamed” (Luk 16:3).
Greek eleemosune (G1654) — alms, mercy shown in a gift; “to ask alms of them that entered into the temple” (Act 3:2).
usage: “yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread” (Psa 37:25) — begging as the mark of the abandoned, not the holy.
“that we might not be chargeable to any of you” (2Th 3:8) — Paul's own practice, deliberately not mendicant.
“having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8) — the standard that judges both begging and hoarding.

pos: n. (a convent of friars; a mendicant house, usually set in a town rather than in the wilderness)
etymology: From friar, Old French frere, Latin frater, a brother; with the place-suffix -y. The brothers' house.
biblical_def: A friary is a house of friars, and its siting tells the whole story of the mendicant movement. The old monasteries were planted in valleys and on moors, deliberately away from men; the friaries were built in towns, in the poorest quarters, next to the markets and the schools. The friars came to preach, and preaching requires hearers: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14), and “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15). In that the friars recovered something the cloister had lost. A friary was not self-sufficient, held little land, and depended on the town it served, which kept it close to ordinary people and gave the orders their early popularity. The defects followed from the same closeness. Friaries competed with parish clergy for burials, confessions and legacies; their preachers were often licensed over the heads of local pastors; and houses vowed to poverty accumulated handsome buildings by gift. Chaucer's friar is not a Protestant slander but a medieval complaint. Still, the impulse that built them — take the word to where the people are — is one Scripture plainly commends.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines friary as a monastery or convent of friars, and as an adjective like a friar; friar as an appellation given to monks who live in convents; and convent as a house for persons devoted to religion, an abbey or monastery.
webster_full: FRIARY, n. A monastery; a convent of friars.
FRIARY, a. Like a friar; pertaining to friars or to a monastery.
FRIAR, n. An appellation common to the monks of all orders; those who live in convents or houses of religious retirement.
CONVENT, n. A house for persons devoted to religion; an abbey; a monastery; a nunnery.
PREACH, v.i. To pronounce a public discourse on a religious subject, or from a text of scripture.
scriptures: How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
corruption_summary: A town convent of friars: the gospel carried to where people actually live, in houses that were vowed to poverty and grew rich by legacy.
corruption_paragraphs: The real corruption of the friaries was institutional hypocrisy, and it was named at the time. Houses sworn to own nothing came to hold fine churches, libraries and rents, received by gift so that the vow might technically stand. Paul's warning about ministry for gain fits exactly: “For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith” (1Ti 6:10). A vow kept by a legal fiction is worse than no vow, because it teaches the conscience to reason in fictions.

The principle to recover is the siting, not the vow. The friars were right that the gospel must be preached where men are, and right that a preacher tied to the rich will flatter them. “How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace” (Rom 10:15) commends the going; nothing in Scripture commends the pretence of destitution that later came with it.
roots_summary: Latin frater, a brother; Greek adelphos (G80), a brother; Greek kerusso (G2784), to proclaim as a herald; Greek euaggelizo (G2097), to bring good news; Hebrew basar (H1319), to bear tidings.
roots_lines: Latin frater — a brother; the friar is a brother rather than a father, which was the point of the name.
Greek adelphos (G80) — brother; “one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8).
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim as a herald; “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2).
Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to announce good news; the verb behind “evangelise”.
Hebrew basar (H1319) — to bear tidings; “the feet of him that bringeth good tidings” (Isa 52:7).
usage: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — the commission the friaries were built to serve.
“how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — the argument for a house in the town rather than the moor.
“For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10) — the reef the friaries struck.

pos: n. and a. (a member of the Order of Friars Minor founded by Francis of Assisi in 1209; of that order)
etymology: From Francis (Latin Franciscus) of Assisi; the order's own name was Ordo Fratrum Minorum, the Order of Lesser Brothers.
biblical_def: The Franciscans are the friars of Francis of Assisi, approved in 1209, who called themselves not the Great but the Lesser Brothers. Their founding texts were taken straight from the gospels: “If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me” (Mat 19:21), and the charge to the Twelve, “Take nothing for your journey, neither staves, nor scrip, neither bread, neither money” (Luk 9:3). Francis read these as a literal rule of life, and the order he left preached barefoot, worked among lepers, and refused property corporately as well as individually. A Protestant must say two things about it. First, the movement recovered real neglected scripture — the gospel preached to the poor, a ministry not for gain, a church visibly unattached to money — and it shamed a wealthy hierarchy by simply obeying. Second, it mistook a commission for a counsel and a means for a merit. Poverty is not holiness; Christ's word to the rich young man exposed an idol in that particular man, and “Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith” (Jam 2:5) speaks of God's election, not of poverty earning anything.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Franciscan as belonging to the order of St Francis, and as a noun one of the order of St Francis, called also Gray Friars and Minorites; and mendicant as one of the begging fraternities of the Romish church.
webster_full: FRANCISCAN, a. Belonging to the order of St. Francis.
FRANCISCAN, n. One of the order of St. Francis; an order of religious, called also Gray Friars, and Minorites.
MINOR, a. Less; smaller; inferior; as the minor part of the society.
POVERTY, n. Destitution of property; indigence; want of convenient means of subsistence.
PERFECT, a. Finished; complete; consummate; not defective; having all that is requisite to its nature and kind.
scriptures: Jesus said unto him, If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me.
Luk 9:3
And he said unto them, Take nothing for your journey, neither staves, nor scrip, neither bread, neither money; neither have two coats apiece.
Jam 2:5
Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?
Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.
corruption_summary: The Friars Minor of Francis of Assisi: a genuine recovery of the gospel preached to the poor, built on a vow that treated poverty itself as merit.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrinal corruption is the merit of poverty, and it is not a small thing. If selling all is the counsel of perfection, then there are two grades of Christian and the gospel has a higher tier for the heroic. Scripture refuses that division. Paul, who knew real destitution — “in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness” (2Co 11:27) — never once counts it toward his standing, and declares his contentment learnt in both conditions: “I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound” (Phi 4:12).

The modern misuse of Francis is to keep him as a sentimental figure of birds and ecology and to drop the Christ he preached. That is a far worse corruption than his vow was. The principle to recover is the one he genuinely saw: a church attached to money cannot preach to the poor, and “Sell that ye have, and give alms” (Luk 12:33) is addressed to disciples who had a great deal more to give than they thought.
roots_summary: Latin minor, lesser; Greek ptochos (G4434), poor; Greek teleios (G5046), complete or perfect; Greek akoloutheo (G190), to follow; Hebrew ani (H6041), afflicted or poor.
roots_lines: Latin fratres minores — lesser brothers; the order's own chosen name, and a rebuke to rank.
Greek teleios (G5046) — complete, mature; “If thou wilt be perfect” (Mat 19:21) — wholeness, not a higher tier.
Greek akoloutheo (G190) — to follow, to accompany as a disciple; the verb of the call.
Greek ptochos (G4434) — the destitute poor, those to whom the gospel is preached.
Hebrew ani (H6041) — poor, afflicted, bowed down; the Psalter's word for the man God hears.
usage: “go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor” (Mat 19:21) — the text Francis read as a rule for all.
“Take nothing for your journey” (Luk 9:3) — a commission for a mission, taken as a permanent vow.
“I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound” (Phi 4:12) — Paul's verdict on both estates.

pos: n. and a. (a member of the order of hermits living under the Rule of Augustine; also, one holding Augustine's doctrine of grace)
etymology: From Augustine of Hippo (Latin Augustinus); the Rule ascribed to him governed both the Hermits and the Canons that bear his name.
biblical_def: The word carries two senses a Protestant must keep apart. Institutionally, the Augustinians are the Order of Hermits of St Augustine, gathered out of several Italian eremitical groups in 1256 and living under a short rule ascribed to Augustine of Hippo. Doctrinally, Augustinian names the theology of grace which Augustine drew out of Paul against Pelagius — that the will is bound until God frees it, that faith is itself a gift, that salvation is of mercy and not of merit: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8), and “And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace” (Rom 11:6). The two senses met in a single friar. Martin Luther was an Augustinian of the order who, reading Paul in an Augustinian's cell, recovered Augustine's doctrine against his own order's practice. That is the irony worth stating plainly: the Reformation came out of this order because its namesake had already taught, from Scripture, what its late-medieval religion of merit denied. “Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Tit 3:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Augustinian as pertaining to St Augustine, and as a noun one of a religious order so named; and grace as the free unmerited love and favor of God, the divine influence which renews the heart.
webster_full: AUGUSTINIAN, a. Pertaining to St. Augustine, bishop of Hippo, or to his doctrines.
AUGUSTINIAN, n. One of a religious order, so called from St. Augustine; also, one who holds the doctrines of Augustine.
GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God; the divine influence which renews the heart of man and restrains from sin.
MERIT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles to honor or reward; worth; value.
HERMIT, n. A person who retires from society and lives in solitude; a recluse; an anchoret.
scriptures: Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Rom 11:6
And if by grace, then is it no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, then is it no more grace: otherwise work is no more work.
Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
Rom 3:28
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law.
corruption_summary: Both an order of friars and a doctrine of grace: the order ran on merit, the doctrine destroys merit, and an Augustinian friar noticed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption lies in the gap between the two senses. An order named for the greatest ancient enemy of works-righteousness had, by 1500, a whole economy of merit: masses said for pay, indulgences, a graded holiness. Augustine's own ground cuts it away — “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28). The name was kept and the theology mislaid, which is a warning to every institution that carries a great man's name.

The modern misuse is to treat Augustinian as a historical label with no claim on anybody, a school among schools. But the doctrine is not a school; it is Paul's plain teaching, and it either stands or the gospel falls. The principle to recover is the sheer gratuity of salvation: “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9).
roots_summary: Greek charis (G5485), grace or favour; Greek doron (G1435), a gift; Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify; Greek ergon (G2041), a work; Hebrew chen (H2580), favour.
roots_lines: Greek charis (G5485) — grace, unearned favour; “if by grace, then is it no more of works” (Rom 11:6).
Greek doron (G1435) — a gift; “it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8).
Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous; “a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28).
Greek ergon (G2041) — a work; the thing Paul excludes from the ground of acceptance.
Hebrew chen (H2580) — favour, grace; what Noah found in the eyes of the LORD before he did anything.
usage: “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8) — the Augustinian doctrine in one sentence.
“Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Tit 3:5) — merit excluded by name.
“otherwise grace is no more grace” (Rom 11:6) — the logic that admits no mixture.

pos: n. pl. (regular canons living in community under the Rule of Augustine, serving churches, hospitals and schools)
etymology: Latin canonici regulares, canons living under a rule; canon from Greek kanon, a rule, with the Rule ascribed to Augustine.
biblical_def: The Augustinian or Austin Canons — the Black Canons — were priests living in community under a rule, and they occupied a position between the monk and the parish clergyman which is worth understanding. A monk withdrew; a canon was ordained and served: his house kept a parish church, a hospital, a bridge, a school, a shrine. Hundreds of such houses dotted medieval England and the Low Countries, and they are the reason so many medieval hospitals existed at all. Their work has solid scriptural warrant. “I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me” (Mat 25:36) is the charter of their infirmaries, and “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27) names the religion they practised better than their own rule did. Their weakness was the common one of the regular clergy: a community of priests under vows is still a community under vows, and the Canons' houses drifted into the same system of appropriated tithes and absentee care that the Reformers attacked. The service was real; the structure that owned it was not accountable to the people it served.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines canon as a dignitary of the church, or an ecclesiastical rule; regular as belonging to a religious order; and hospital as a building appropriated for the reception of sick, infirm and helpless paupers.
webster_full: CANON, n. An ecclesiastical law, or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign.
CANON, n. A dignitary of the church; a person who possesses a prebend or revenue allotted for the performance of divine service in a cathedral or collegiate church.
REGULAR, a. In a monastic sense, belonging to a religious order, or bound by the rules of a monastic institution.
HOSPITAL, n. A building appropriated for the reception of sick, infirm and helpless paupers, who are supported and nursed by charity.
VISIT, v.t. To go or come to see; to attend, as a physician; to go to with care and relief, as the sick and afflicted.
scriptures: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.

Well reported of for good works; if she have brought up children, if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted, if she have diligently followed every good work.
Isa 58:7

Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house? when thou seest the naked, that thou cover him; and that thou hide not thyself from thine own flesh?
corruption_summary: Ordained canons in community, running the parishes, hospitals and schools: genuine mercy, held inside a structure answerable to its order and not its people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the care of the sick, the stranger and the orphan is religion and not an optional extra — “Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?” (Isa 58:7) — and the Canons did this on a scale modern churches rarely attempt.

The live defect is the one every institutional charity faces: the work outlasts the faith that began it, and the house becomes a landlord. Appropriated tithes meant a canonry drew a parish's income while a poorly paid vicar did its work. “if she have lodged strangers, if she have washed the saints' feet, if she have relieved the afflicted” (1Ti 5:10) describes hands-on mercy, which is not the same as endowing it.
roots_summary: Greek kanon (G2583), a rule; Greek episkopeo (G1983), to oversee; Greek diakonia (G1248), ministry or service; Hebrew chesed (H2617), covenant mercy; Greek xenodocheo from xenos (G3581), a stranger.
roots_lines: Greek kanon (G2583) — a rule; the canons are named for living by one.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministry; the New Testament word for exactly the Canons' work.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — steadfast covenant mercy; the quality their hospitals embodied at their best.
Greek xenos (G3581) — a stranger or guest; “if she have lodged strangers” (1Ti 5:10).
Greek episkopeo (G1983) — to oversee, to look upon with care; the duty of an ordained canon toward his parish.
usage: “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36) — the charter of the Canons' hospitals.
“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jam 1:27) — religion defined as the Canons practised it.
“Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry” (Isa 58:7) — the fast God chooses, and the work a canonry owed.

pos: n. and a. (a friar of the stricter branch, holding the rule as written; of that reform)
etymology: Latin observare, to watch, heed or keep; the Observants are those who keep the rule rather than its dispensations.
biblical_def: An Observant is a friar of the strict branch — chiefly among the Franciscans, where the order split formally in 1517 into Observants and Conventuals over whether the rule of poverty meant what it said. The Observants held it did. They refused corporate property, kept the fasts, and reformed house after house back to the founder's letter; the Conventuals accepted papal dispensations that let the order hold goods through trustees. The dispute is instructive for Protestants, because both parties were partly right and the frame of the question was wrong. The Observants were right that a vow dispensed into meaninglessness is a lie, and that God hates a kept form with an evaded substance: “Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams” (1Sa 15:22). What neither side could ask was whether the rule should bind at all. Observance is a virtue only toward what God has commanded; strictness toward a human rule is the very thing Paul calls “a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23). Rigour about the wrong law is not holiness, however sincere, and the Observants proved that a reform can be real and still not be the Reformation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines observant as attentive, watchful, and carefully attentive to the performance of rites or duties; observance as the act of keeping a law or custom; and strict as exact, rigorously nice.
webster_full: OBSERVANT, a. Taking notice; attentive; watchful; also, carefully attentive; submissive; obedient.
OBSERVANCE, n. The act of observing; performance, as the observance of a law or rule; also, a ceremony or rite.
OBSERVE, v.t. To keep religiously; to celebrate; as, to observe a feast or a fast.
STRICT, a. Exact; rigorously nice; observing exact rules; severe; not loose or vague.
DISPENSATION, n. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by laws or canons.
scriptures: And Samuel said, Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.
Col 2:23
Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.

Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
corruption_summary: The strict branch of the friars: right that a dispensed vow is a lie, unable to ask whether the vow bound at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption the Observants rightly attacked was dispensation — a rule formally retained and practically annulled by permission. That is the sin of the lawyer's conscience, and Christ named it: “ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith” (Mat 23:23). A vow evaded by a legal device teaches a man that God can be managed.

The corruption the Observants could not see is in the word itself. Observance of what God commands is obedience; observance of a self-imposed rule, however rigorous, is “will worship” (Col 2:23). The principle to recover is the simplicity of what is actually required: “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Mic 6:8).
roots_summary: Latin observare, to keep or heed; Hebrew shamar (H8104), to keep or guard; Greek tereo (G5083), to keep; Greek phulasso (G5442), to guard; Hebrew shama (H8085), to hear and obey.
roots_lines: Latin observare — to watch, heed, keep; the branch is named for keeping the rule as written.
Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, watch, guard; the Old Testament word for keeping God's commandments.
Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear, and so to obey; “to hearken than the fat of rams” (1Sa 15:22).
Greek tereo (G5083) — to keep, to observe; used of keeping Christ's commandments, never of keeping a human rule.
Greek phulasso (G5442) — to guard, to keep safe; the stricter sense of custody.
usage: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1Sa 15:22) — the Observants' best argument, and its limit.
“have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith” (Mat 23:23) — rigour misdirected.
“to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8) — the rule that needs no dispensation.

pos: n. and a. (a friar of the branch holding property under dispensation; of or belonging to a convent)
etymology: Latin conventus, an assembly or coming together, from convenire, to come together; the convent is the gathered body, and a conventual belongs to it.
biblical_def: A Conventual is, first, simply a member of a convent; second, and more pointedly, a friar of the branch which accepted papal dispensations permitting the order to hold property through trustees. The Conventual case was practical and not contemptible: a house must be housed, books must be kept, the sick must be fed, and a literal destitution makes a settled ministry impossible. Scripture does provide for the support of ministers — “Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1Co 9:14) — and “the workman is worthy of his meat” (Mat 10:10). The Conventuals had the better of the argument about facts and the worse of it about honesty. They kept the vow's words and emptied its meaning, and the fiction of a trustee holding what the order used is exactly the kind of oath-management Christ forbade when he told men to swear not at all but to let “let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Mat 5:37). The clean resolution was neither branch's: own what you own, say so, and do not vow what you do not mean.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conventual as belonging to a convent or monastic; as a noun, a monk or nun, one that lives in a convent; and convent as a house for persons devoted to religion.
webster_full: CONVENTUAL, a. Belonging to a convent; monastic; as conventual priors.
CONVENTUAL, n. A monk or nun; one that lives in a convent.
CONVENT, n. A house for persons devoted to religion; an abbey; a monastery; a nunnery.
TRUSTEE, n. A person to whom property is legally committed in trust, to be applied to a particular use.
PROPERTY, n. The exclusive right of possessing, enjoying and disposing of a thing; ownership.
scriptures: Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.
Nor scrip for your journey, neither two coats, neither shoes, nor yet staves: for the workman is worthy of his meat.
Mat 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
Ecc 5:5
Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
corruption_summary: The property-holding branch of the friars: right that ministry needs support, wrong to keep a vow's words while a trustee held what the vow renounced.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is the managed oath. A vow of poverty satisfied by having another man hold the title is a vow in form only, and Scripture is severe about exactly this: “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5). The Conventuals did not fall by owning things; they fell by swearing not to and then owning them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is plain speech about money in the church. “they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1Co 9:14) is permission to be supported openly; it is not cover for an endowment behind a pretence of destitution, and a church that is frank about its finances is nearer the apostles than one that is pious about them.
roots_summary: Latin conventus, an assembly; Hebrew neder (H5088), a vow; Greek euche (G2171), a vow or prayer; Greek sunagoge (G4864), a gathering together; Greek oikonomia (G3622), stewardship.
roots_lines: Latin conventus — a coming together; the convent is the gathered body, the conventual its member.
Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow, a thing promised to God; “Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5).
Greek euche (G2171) — a vow; the New Testament keeps the Old Testament's gravity about it.
Greek oikonomia (G3622) — stewardship, the management of a household's goods.
Greek sunagoge (G4864) — a gathering together; the Greek counterpart of conventus.
usage: “they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel” (1Co 9:14) — the Conventuals' sound point.
“Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay” (Ecc 5:5) — the verdict on the device.
“let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay” (Mat 5:37) — the plainness that would have settled the quarrel.

pos: n. (a friar of the Capuchin reform of the Franciscans, 1528, named from the pointed hood of their habit)
etymology: Italian cappuccino, from cappuccio, a hood or cowl; the reform took its popular name from the long pointed hood its friars wore.
biblical_def: The Capuchins are a Franciscan reform of 1528, begun by Matteo da Bascio in a search for the founder's original austerity, and named by the people for the long pointed hood they wore. They became the most effective preachers and the most conspicuous plague-nurses of the Catholic Reformation, going barefoot, keeping to a severe poverty, and working in epidemics where others fled. Honesty requires a Protestant to grant the courage. Nursing the plague-stricken is “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36) done at the risk of life, and the Capuchins did it when the gentry had left town. It requires equal honesty to say what they were for. The order was a front line of the Counter-Reformation, formed to win back by preaching and self-denial what Rome had lost by corruption, and the gospel it preached kept the merit, the mass and the mediation of saints that the Reformers had found no warrant for. Courage does not settle doctrine. “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) is written against heroic preachers as much as lazy ones.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives capuchin as a female garment resembling the habit of a capuchin friar, and notes the Capuchins as monks of the order of St Francis who wear a cowl or capuche; and hood as a covering for the head.
webster_full: CAPUCHIN, n. A garment for females, consisting of a cloak and hood, made in imitation of the dress of Capuchin monks.
CAPUCHIN, n. One of a religious order of the strict observance of St. Francis, who wear a capuche or pointed hood.
CAPUCHE, n. A monk's hood; a cowl.
HOOD, n. A covering for the head, used by females, and formerly worn by men; also, the cowl of a monk.
AUSTERITY, n. Severity of manners or life; rigor; strictness; harsh discipline.
scriptures: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Jam 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
corruption_summary: The barefoot Franciscan reform of 1528: real courage in the plague wards, in the service of a gospel that kept the merit the Reformers had removed.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is doctrinal rather than moral, and it is the harder kind to see because the lives were good. A reform that recovers austerity without recovering justification has recovered the wrong thing: the Capuchins preached self-denial as a way toward God, where Paul writes “a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). Sincerity and severity are not evidence of a true gospel; they are what makes a false one persuasive.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Capuchins' practice without their doctrine: Christians who stay in the plague city. “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world” (Jam 1:27) — and Protestants who concede the courage should ask why it so often had to be conceded.
roots_summary: Italian cappuccio, a hood; Greek euaggelion (G2098), gospel; Greek pistis (G4102), faith; Greek askesis, training or discipline; Hebrew chesed (H2617), mercy.
roots_lines: Italian cappuccio — a hood; the name the Italian poor gave the friars from their one visible peculiarity.
Greek euaggelion (G2098) — good news; “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel” (Gal 1:8).
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, trust; “but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16).
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, loyal love; the virtue of the plague wards.
Greek egkrateia (G1466) — self-control; a fruit of the Spirit, not a ladder to him.
usage: “I was sick, and ye visited me” (Mat 25:36) — done at the risk of life, which the Capuchins did.
“a man is not justified by the works of the law” (Gal 2:16) — the doctrine the austerity could not supply.
“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — a judgment on the message, whatever the messenger's courage.

pos: n. (a Friar Minor; a Franciscan, from the order's own title Fratres Minores)
etymology: Latin minor, lesser; the Order of Friars Minor, Ordo Fratrum Minorum, a name Francis chose so that his brothers should be the lesser and not the greater.
biblical_def: Minorite is the older English name for a Franciscan, taken from the order's own title: Friars Minor, the Lesser Brothers. The choice of name was deliberate and it is the best thing about the order. Francis would not have his men be maiores, the greater, the term for the ruling class of an Italian town; they were to be the lesser, ranked below. That instinct is straight out of the gospels. “whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26); “whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted” (Luk 14:11); and the refusal of titles, “But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8). In England the Minorites gave their name to streets and districts where their houses stood, and their early reputation was for learning as well as poverty — Grosseteste taught them, and Ockham and Bacon came out of them. The irony the name invites is that an order constituted as the lesser came to hold chairs, bishoprics and the ear of princes. Humility written into a constitution does not stay there by itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines minor as less, smaller, inferior; minorite as a Franciscan friar; and minister as one who serves, an agent acting under another, and in religion one who serves at the altar or preaches.
webster_full: MINORITE, n. A Franciscan friar; one of the order of Friars Minor.
MINOR, a. Less; smaller; inferior; as the minor part of the society.
MINISTER, n. One who serves; a servant; an agent acting under the authority of another; one to whom a sovereign commits the administration of government.
MINISTER, n. One who serves at the altar; one who performs sacerdotal duties; the pastor of a church, duly authorized to preach the gospel.
HUMBLE, a. Low; opposed to high or lofty; modest; meek; submissive; having a low opinion of one's self.
scriptures: But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
Mat 23:8
But be not ye called Rabbi: for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
Phi 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
corruption_summary: The Lesser Brothers: a name chosen to put the friars below everyone, borne by an order that came to hold chairs and bishoprics.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the slow reversal of a name. An order constituted as minores ended with cardinals in it, which is not a scandal peculiar to Rome but the ordinary gravity of institutions. Paul's remedy is not a title but a habit of mind: “Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves” (Phi 2:3). Lowliness that has to be codified has usually already gone.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Francis saw in the gospels and stated in a name: Christian greatness is service and nothing else. “whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26) — and every church that builds a platform should read it again.
roots_summary: Latin minor, lesser; Greek diakonos (G1249), a servant; Greek tapeinophrosune (G5012), lowliness of mind; Greek adelphos (G80), brother; Hebrew anav (H6035), humble.
roots_lines: Latin minor — lesser; the whole argument of the order's name.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant, one who waits on another; “let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26).
Greek tapeinophrosune (G5012) — lowliness of mind; “in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves” (Phi 2:3).
Greek adelphos (G80) — brother; “all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8).
Hebrew anav (H6035) — humble, afflicted, meek; the word of Moses and of the Messiah.
usage: “But be not ye called Rabbi” (Mat 23:8) — the text behind the choice of the name.
“he that humbleth himself shall be exalted” (Luk 14:11) — the promise, and the warning against engineering it.
“in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves” (Phi 2:3) — lowliness as a practice, not a title.

pos: n. (a member of a Third Order: a layman living under a mendicant rule adapted to life in the world)
etymology: Latin tertiarius, of the third, from tertius, third; the Third Order after the friars (first) and the enclosed sisters (second).
biblical_def: A tertiary is a layman or laywoman affiliated to a mendicant order under a rule adapted for life in the world: married, working, keeping a trade, but bound to set prayers, fasts, simplicity of dress and works of mercy. The Third Orders were among the most popular religious movements of the later Middle Ages, and for good reason. They answered a real hunger of ordinary believers who had been taught that serious discipleship happened in cloisters and who could not enter one. The answer Scripture gives to that hunger is better than a third order, and it is the doctrine the Reformation recovered: there is no higher Christian estate to join. The baptised farmer is already a priest — “ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people” (1Pe 2:9) — and his ordinary work is already the service of God: “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23). The tertiary movement is the medieval church conceding, under pressure from the laity, a truth its own structure denied; and conceding it by halves, with a lesser rule for lesser Christians.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tertiary as third in order, and third as the ordinal of three; layman as a man who is not a clergyman; and vocation as a calling by the will of God, or the employment in which one is engaged.
webster_full: TERTIARY, a. Third in order or formation; of the third order or rank.
THIRD, a. The first after the second; the ordinal of three.
LAYMAN, n. A man who is not a clergyman; one of the laity or people distinct from the clergy.
VOCATION, n. A calling by the will of God; also, employment; calling; occupation; trade; the business of a man's life.
ORDER, n. A religious fraternity; as the order of Franciscans; a body of men united by some common bond or rule.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Brethren, let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God.
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
corruption_summary: Lay members under a mendicant rule: a real answer to a real hunger, offered as a third tier where Scripture gives the laity the first.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the tiering itself. A system that makes the cloister the serious option and then invents a junior membership for everyone else has taught the laity that their baptism was not enough. Paul will not have it: “let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24) — the calling a man is already in is the place of his obedience, requiring no affiliation to upgrade it.

The modern misuse is the same structure under new management: a tier of the specially committed, marked by a programme or a rule, against which the ordinary member measures short. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of the plain Christian life. “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) is an apostolic command, and it describes almost nobody's idea of a higher calling.
roots_summary: Latin tertius, third; Greek klesis (G2821), a calling; Greek laos (G2992), a people; Greek hierateuma (G2406), a priesthood; Hebrew am (H5971), a people.
roots_lines: Latin tertiarius — of the third; the rank the movement was given in its own system.
Greek laos (G2992) — a people; the root of “laity”, and in the New Testament a word of dignity, not of rank.
Greek hierateuma (G2406) — a priesthood; “a royal priesthood, an holy nation” (1Pe 2:9).
Greek klesis (G2821) — a calling; “let every man, wherein he is called, therein abide with God” (1Co 7:24).
Hebrew am (H5971) — a people, the congregation as a whole; never a lower order within it.
usage: “ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9) — said to the whole church, which ends the tiering.
“whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord” (Col 3:23) — the ordinary trade as service to God.
“to work with your own hands” (1Th 4:11) — an apostolic rule of life, with no order to join.
